chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Statistical Toolkit — Correlation, Spread, and Z-Score

lessons.title: Building a Spread: Price Ratios vs Regression-Based Hedge Ratios

children.text: Lesson 2 introduced the spread as the actual asset a stat arb trade is built on. What it did not cover is how exactly you build one. There are two common ways, and the difference between them is not a minor technical detail. One of them can quietly embed a trend into your spread that has nothing to do with mean reversion at all.

body.text: A price ratio is the simplest way to build a spread, but it silently assumes the two prices move in exact fixed proportion, with no constant offset between them. A regression-based hedge ratio makes no such assumption, and produces a cleaner, more genuinely stable spread as a result.

children.text: The price ratio, Stock A's price divided by Stock B's price, is what Lesson 2 used, and it is a perfectly reasonable place to start screening candidate pairs. It is also, mathematically, a fairly strong assumption: it assumes Price A equals some constant multiple of Price B and nothing else, as if the relationship between the two passes exactly through zero. If that assumption happens to be roughly true, the ratio spread works fine. If it is not, and in practice it usually is not exactly true, the ratio spread can drift over time in a way that looks like a trend, even when the two stocks' underlying relationship has not actually changed at all.

markDefs.definition: The number of units, or the rupee sensitivity, of one asset held against another so a combined position responds to their shared driver in a controlled way. In a regression-based spread, this is the fitted slope, beta.

children.text: The more careful approach is to fit a linear regression of one stock's price on the other, and use the fitted slope as the

, with the regression's residual, the leftover, unexplained part, becoming the spread itself. Unlike the plain ratio, this approach allows for a constant offset between the two prices, and lets the data tell you the actual historical sensitivity between them, rather than assuming it is exactly 1:1 in ratio terms.

body.caption: The spread is the regression residual: whatever part of Y is left over after removing the part explained by X. Beta is estimated by ordinary least squares: β = Σ(xᵢ-x̄)(yᵢ-ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ-x̄)²

children.text: Seeing the Difference: A Worked Example
Here are eight illustrative daily closing prices for ICICI Bank and HDFC Bank, constructed so that HDFC's relationship to ICICI includes a meaningful constant offset, not just a simple multiple.

body.caption: Illustrative daily closes: ICICI Bank vs HDFC Bank

body.code:
import numpy as np

icici = np.array([800, 830, 860, 890, 920, 950, 980, 1000])
hdfc = np.array([1323, 1360, 1408, 1443, 1490, 1526, 1575, 1599])

beta, alpha = np.polyfit(icici, hdfc, 1)
residuals = hdfc - (alpha + beta * icici)

print("beta:", round(beta, 4))
print("alpha:", round(alpha, 2))
print("residuals:", np.round(residuals, 2))
body.caption: Fitting the hedge ratio with numpy's polyfit and computing the regression residual spread

body.label: Hedge ratio (β) from this regression
body.context: Interpreted as: for every ₹1 move in ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank has historically moved about ₹1.39, based on this fitted relationship, not a fixed price ratio. The fitted intercept, α ≈ 208, is exactly the constant offset the ratio method ignores.

body.title: The naive ratio spread (HDFC ÷ ICICI) drifts (illustrative)
The regression residual spread stays flat (illustrative)

body.text: Same eight days, same two stocks. The ratio spread drifts steadily downward, from about 1.654 to 1.599, a roughly 3 percent move that has nothing to do with mean reversion, it is purely an artifact of ignoring the constant offset between the two prices. The regression residual spread has no such drift; it oscillates in a tight band around zero, which is exactly the behavior Lesson 3 described as mean-reverting.

children.text: Which Method Should You Actually Use?

columns.label: Price Ratio Spread
points: Fast to compute, no estimation required
Fine for a first, rough screen of candidate pairs
Silently assumes no constant offset between the two prices
Can show a fake trend if that assumption doesn't hold

columns.label: Regression-Based Hedge Ratio Spread
points: Requires fitting a regression, one extra step
Accounts for a constant offset between the two prices
Produces a spread that is a better candidate for the mean-reversion and cointegration tests in Chapter 3
The standard approach used before sizing and trading a real pair

body.text: A hedge ratio estimated once and never revisited is itself a simplification. The true relationship between two stocks can drift gradually over months, which means a β estimated from last year's data may not be the right hedge ratio today. Chapter 5 covers the Kalman filter, a way to let the hedge ratio update itself continuously instead of staying fixed.

body.title: Why did the ratio spread drift?
body.question: In the worked example above, the ratio spread (HDFC ÷ ICICI) drifted from about 1.654 down to 1.599 over the eight days, even though the underlying relationship between the two stocks did not actually change. What caused this drift?
options: HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank stopped being correlated
The true relationship between the two prices includes a constant offset that the ratio method ignores
There was a data error in the price series
The regression method is wrong and the ratio method is correct
body.explanation: The ratio method implicitly assumes Y is a pure multiple of X with no constant offset. When the true relationship includes a meaningful constant term, as it did here, the ratio drifts as the price level changes, even though nothing about the real relationship has shifted. The regression method, which explicitly estimates that constant, does not have this problem.

body.title: Apply the hedge ratio
body.prompt: Using the fitted hedge ratio β ≈ 1.39 from this lesson's worked example, if ICICI Bank moves up by ₹10, how many rupees would you expect HDFC Bank to move, on average, based on this hedge ratio?
body.explanation: The hedge ratio β tells you the average rupee move in Y (HDFC) per ₹1 move in X (ICICI). ₹10 × 1.39 ≈ ₹13.9.

cards.definition: A spread built by dividing one stock's price by another's. Simple to compute, but implicitly assumes the two prices are related by a fixed multiple with no constant offset.

The number of units, or the rupee sensitivity, of one asset held against another so their combined position responds to a shared driver in a controlled way. In a regression-based spread, this is the fitted slope, beta.
A spread built as the residual from regressing one stock's price on another, Y minus its predicted value. Accounts for a constant offset between the two prices, unlike a simple ratio.
The standard method for fitting a regression line by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, used here to estimate the hedge ratio beta.

points: A spread can be built as a simple price ratio, or as the residual from a regression of one stock's price on the other. The two are not the same thing.

The price ratio implicitly assumes no constant offset between the two prices. When that assumption fails, the ratio spread can drift in a way that looks like a trend, even when the underlying relationship is stable.

A regression-based spread, Y minus its predicted value from X, explicitly accounts for a constant offset and gives a data-driven hedge ratio, beta, producing a cleaner residual to test for mean reversion.
The hedge ratio beta tells you how many rupees one stock has historically moved for every ₹1 move in the other. It is not the same number as the simple price ratio between them.
A hedge ratio estimated once can go stale as the relationship between two stocks drifts. Chapter 5's Kalman filter addresses this by updating the hedge ratio continuously.
